back: A subword piece from the tokenizer's fixed vocabulary. Rule of thumb for English: about 4 characters or 0.75 words per token. All LLM limits and prices are in tokens.
One parallel forward pass over all prompt tokens. Compute-bound. Produces the first token and fills the KV cache.
Generates one token per step per sequence. Each step reads every weight from memory, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound.

front: Batch-1 decode bound for a 7B fp16 model at 2 TB/s (assumed)?
back: 13.5 GB of weights ÷ 2,000 GB/s ≈ 6.7 ms per token, so at most about 150 tokens/s for one user.

front: KV cache bytes per token formula?
back: 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value. Llama 2 7B in fp16: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 512 KiB.

front: Why does Llama 2 70B have a smaller KV cache per token than 7B?
back: Grouped-query attention: 64 query heads share 8 KV heads, so 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 320 KiB per token.

front: What usually decides how many requests fit on a GPU?
back: Free memory for the KV cache after weights and overhead, divided by tokens per request. Not the weights alone.
The batch runs until its longest request finishes, so short requests hold idle slots and new arrivals wait outside.
Iteration-level scheduling: at every decode step, finished sequences leave and waiting requests join.
KV cache stored in fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default) with a per-sequence block table, like virtual memory pages. No up-front reservation; prefixes can be shared.

front: What happens in vLLM when KV blocks run out?
back: The scheduler preempts requests (by default the most recently admitted), dropping their KV to recompute later or swapping it to CPU.
Time to first token: queueing + prefill + first decode step. Driven by prompt length and scheduler load.
Time per output token (inter-token latency). Driven by decode speed and batch size. Per-user tokens/s = 1 ÷ TPOT.

front: End-to-end latency of a streamed answer?
back: ≈ TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × TPOT. 0.4 s + 499 × 25 ms ≈ 12.9 s for 500 tokens.
Hourly GPU cost ÷ (tokens/s × 3,600 × utilisation) × 1,000,000. Utilisation is the lever.
Data must stay in your network, or traffic is steady and high enough to keep GPUs busy with an open model that passes your evals.
